title: Loving yourself rightly
hookLine: as yourself assumes you care for yourself too

cards: A king and a queen are talking privately, and the king asks her a question that sounds almost dangerous. Is there anyone, he says, dearer to you than yourself? A careful wife might be expected to say: you, my lord.
She doesn't. She says no, there is no one dearer to her than herself, and then she asks him the same question. He gives the same answer.
Then the king goes to the Buddha and tells him what they said. What the Buddha does with their honesty is the surprise.

teach.b: First, the story. It comes from the Pali scriptures, and the couple are King Pasenadi of Kosala and Queen Mallika. When the king brings their conversation to the Buddha, the Buddha doesn't scold either of them.
He answers with a short verse. In plain words: search in every direction with your mind, and you will find no one dearer to anyone than their own self. Second, the turn.
Because each person holds themselves dear in just this way, the verse says, one who loves oneself should not harm another. Self-love, here, isn't the opposite of kindness. It's the doorway.
Each person knows from the inside how much they want to be safe and well, and that knowledge is the teacher. Third, the Torah makes a similar move.
Leviticus says, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." As thyself. The command assumes a self being loved, a measure already in place.
If the measure is broken, the neighbor gets a broken measure too.

Fourth, the Jewish sage Hillel, who held both sides at once, is remembered in the Mishnah for three questions. In plain words: if I am not for myself, who will be for me? And if I am only for myself, what am I?
And if not now, when? The first makes room for caring for yourself. The second keeps it from shrinking into selfishness.
Rightly, then, means both: loving yourself enough to rest, to eat, to forgive your own mistakes, and remembering that everyone else is doing the very same, from the inside.

how: In Buddhaghosa's instructions, loving-kindness practice begins by wishing oneself well before widening to others, and Jews study Hillel's sayings in Pirkei Avot, the Mishnah's collection of the sages' teachings.

o: a queen the Buddha scolded for being too selfish
the queen who said no one was dearer to her than herself
a queen who said her king was dearer than her own life

games.q: who said what about the self — tap the pairs.
p: so one should not harm another
if I am not for myself, who will be?

s: in the story, the Buddha scolds the queen for being selfish
he answers with a verse: no one is dearer to anyone than themselves, so one should not harm another.
Hillel's questions include "if I am only for myself, what am I?"
his second question keeps self-care from shrinking into selfishness.
"as thyself" in Leviticus leaves the self out
the command assumes a self that is loved, and uses it as the measure.

games.q: you're Queen Mallika. the king asks if anyone is dearer to you than yourself. what do you say?
o: no, no one is dearer to me than myself.
games.why: she says no one is dearer than herself, and asks him the same. the Buddha doesn't scold them: he turns it into a reason not to harm anyone.

practice: Place a hand on your chest or your stomach, feel its warmth, and notice whatever wish to be well is there, rested, safe, understood: a wish that isn't selfish, just human.
Still with your hand there, let one other face come to mind, and remember that they want exactly the same thing, just as much, from the inside.
If you pray, you can ask for both of you to be well, in words your tradition already has.

wordCard.voice: Queen Mallika. Who told her husband the king that no one is dearer to her than herself, and heard the Buddha agree. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: the self, oneself, the word at the center of the Buddha's verse to the king.

carryVoice: Your line: me too. Everyone you pass wants that too. Day eight hundred seventy, done.

sources.q: thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself
